detailed_rationale:
Vedanta Ltd has just completed India's largest corporate demerger: NCLT Mumbai sanctioned the scheme (order dated 16 Dec 2025, widely reported as final approval 9 Jan 2026), the scheme went ex-date 30 Apr 2026 (record date 1 May 2026), and the four spun-off entities - Vedanta Aluminium Metal, Vedanta Oil & Gas (formerly Malco Energy/Cairn), Vedanta Power (formerly Talwandi Sabo Power) and Vedanta Iron & Steel - began trading on NSE/BSE (T2T segment, first 10 sessions) on 15 June 2026. What is left in the listed VEDL shell is a much smaller, focused zinc-silver-copper-critical-minerals holding company anchored by its ~63.4% stake in Hindustan Zinc (HZL), plus Zinc International, copper, nickel (Nicomet) and ferrochrome (FACOR). Residual net debt is reported at only ~$1bn (~0.4x leverage) versus the old conglomerate's multi-billion-dollar consolidated debt - a genuine, verified de-risking of the balance sheet. HZL itself just delivered a record FY26: revenue ₹40,844cr (+20% YoY), EBITDA a record ₹22,162cr (+27% YoY, 54% margin, US$2,508mn), net profit ₹13,832cr (+34%), free cash flow ₹13,337cr, mined-metal output a record 1,114KT, and zinc cost of production down to a 5-year low of $959/t (silver contributed 45% of profit). At ₹257.9/share (16 Jul 2026), market cap is ~₹1,00,849cr; the commonly-quoted trailing PE of 5.69 is a stale artifact computed against pre-demerger consolidated EPS and should not be trusted for the new, much smaller entity - sell-side targets have accordingly reset from a pre-demerger whole-company ~₹864 down to a post-demerger continuing-ops range of roughly ₹308-387.

The real analysis, per our mandate, is capital structure and governance, not the metal cycle. The demerger simplified the org chart but did not remove the extraction mechanism that has defined Vedanta for years: the brand fee paid by the Indian listed subsidiaries up to the UK parent, Vedanta Resources (VRL). Viceroy Research's July 2025 report calculated HZL alone paid ~₹1,562cr in brand fees over FY23-25 (a ~₹2,000cr/year run-rate) that flowed HZL->VEDL->VRL, allegedly without the disinterested-shareholder approval a material related-party transaction requires under SEBI rules. This is not just an activist's claim taken on faith - the Enforcement Directorate already forced Vedanta to refund ₹1,030cr of brand fee to VEDL in 2023 after finding the same pattern problematic once before, i.e., regulators have substantiated this exact extraction mechanism in the past. Layered on top: India's income-tax department has made an adverse GAAR finding that VRL's Mauritius holding vehicle (Vedanta Holdings Mauritius 2 Ltd) was structured mainly to avoid tax (~₹1,308cr exposure, flagged by Viceroy even as NCLT cleared the demerger); a shareholder has an active intervention application before the Supreme Court challenging the brand-fee arrangement as excessive and opaque; and VEDL keeps diluting its stake in its own best asset - a 1.59% HZL stake sale via OFS in January 2026, with a further ~2% government stake sale in HZL reportedly under DIPAM consideration (HZL says it has received no formal communication). Separately, on 14 April 2026 a boiler explosion at the group's Athena Thermal Power Plant in Chhattisgarh killed roughly 20-24 workers and injured 30+ (equipment reportedly sourced from a Chinese manufacturer rather than BHEL); Viceroy's follow-up report tied the incident to a pattern of systemic ESG/safety disregard, and the company's response (that it involved subcontractor personnel, investigation ongoing) did not substantively engage that allegation.

At the parent level there is real, agency-verified progress: VRL net debt is down to $4.9bn (from $8.9bn five years ago) with a target of $3bn by FY27, Moody's upgraded VRL's corporate family rating to Ba3 from B1 and S&P upgraded to 'BB' from 'B+' (14 May 2026), and VRL has lined up a $5.2bn refinancing intended to cut funding costs by up to ~300bps. That progress reduces, but does not eliminate, the pressure to extract cash from the Indian subsidiaries. On our reverse-DCF, VEDL's EV (~₹1,09,000cr = ~₹1,00,849cr market cap + ~₹8,300cr net debt) against an estimated residual EBITDA run-rate (63.4% of HZL's ₹22,162cr ≈ ₹14,050cr, plus copper/nickel/ferrochrome/Zinc International - our estimate, company does not disclose this split at this granularity - roughly ₹16,000-19,000cr all-in) implies ~5.7-6.8x EV/EBITDA. That looks statistically undemanding for a 50%+-margin, 0.4x-levered business, but the EBITDA base is a cyclical peak (record silver contribution, a just-achieved 5-year-low cost base) rather than a normalized run-rate; cycle-adjusted, the multiple looks closer to fair value than to cheap. Management's own $5bn group-EBITDA-by-2030 target requires more than doubling the current base and rests on a 'zinc+lead to 3 million tonnes by 2031' volume goal that has slipped for a decade, plus early-stage, non-earning bets (critical minerals, displays/electronics).
recommendation_rationale: We call Sell rather than Hold because the balance of evidence is negative, not neutral: the demerger removed conglomerate complexity but left the brand-fee extraction mechanism intact, and that mechanism has already once been substantiated by a regulator (the 2023 ED-forced refund is a fact, not an allegation). On top of that sits an unresolved GAAR tax-avoidance finding against the parent's offshore structure, a live Supreme Court PIL on the brand fee itself, a fatal industrial accident that has reopened the ESG/safety critique with an active short-seller amplifying it, and continuous dilution of VEDL's claim on its own best asset (HZL) via OFS with a further government sale under discussion. A 'Hold' would require us to be comfortable underwriting this entire unresolved list on top of ordinary commodity-cycle risk, and we are not - especially since the current 5.7-6.8x EV/EBITDA is only cheap-looking if one does not cycle-adjust for a peak-silver, trough-cost year. We are not calling this a governance-driven zero or predicting a collapse - HZL's operating business is genuinely strong and the parent's deleveraging is real - but on a risk-adjusted basis we don't think investors are being paid enough at current prices to carry the overhang, so we prefer Sell to Hold.
summary: Vedanta completed its long-planned demerger this year: aluminium, oil & gas, power and iron & steel are now separately listed companies (trading since 15 June 2026), and what remains in Vedanta Ltd is a leaner zinc-silver-copper business built around its roughly 63.4% stake in Hindustan Zinc, carrying far less debt than the old conglomerate. Hindustan Zinc itself just posted a record year - strong margins and its lowest-ever zinc production cost - so the core asset is genuinely performing well. But the concerns that dogged Vedanta before the split haven't gone away: the UK parent still draws large 'brand fee' payments from the Indian businesses to help service its own debt (a practice regulators have already once forced it to partly reverse), a tax authority has flagged the parent's overseas holding structure as designed mainly to avoid tax, a shareholder has taken the brand-fee issue to the Supreme Court, and a fatal boiler explosion at a group power plant in April 2026 has reopened questions about safety and governance discipline. Vedanta also keeps selling down its stake in Hindustan Zinc - its best asset - to raise cash, and the government is weighing a further stake sale too. We don't see current prices as compensating investors enough for this unresolved list of governance, tax and safety issues layered on top of normal metal-price cyclicality. We rate it Sell.
positive_para: The demerger is done, not just promised - four entities are already listed and trading, and Vedanta Ltd is now a simpler, higher-margin business than the sprawling conglomerate it used to be. Its core asset, Hindustan Zinc (63.4% owned), delivered a record FY26: revenue up 20% to ₹40,844cr, EBITDA up 27% to a record ₹22,162cr at a 54% margin, and its lowest-ever zinc production cost of $959/tonne, with silver providing a strong additional profit kicker. The residual entity's balance sheet is light (~$1bn net debt, ~0.4x leverage), a sharp improvement on the old Vedanta. At the parent level, Vedanta Resources has cut net debt from $8.9bn to $4.9bn over five years, earned rating upgrades from both Moody's (to Ba3) and S&P (to BB) in May 2026, and lined up a $5.2bn refinancing expected to cut funding costs by up to 300bps - real, agency-verified deleveraging. On reported numbers the stock is not expensive, and management's stated ambitions (3 million tonnes zinc+lead by 2031, $5bn group EBITDA by 2030, critical-minerals optionality) offer a path to a materially larger business if even partly delivered.
negative_para: The strongest bear point is that the demerger simplified the org chart without touching the mechanism that has drained value to the parent for years - the brand fee. Viceroy Research calculated HZL alone paid ~₹1,562cr in brand fees over FY23-25 (a ~₹2,000cr/year run-rate) flowing to VEDL and onward to VRL, allegedly without the disinterested-shareholder vote a material related-party transaction requires - and this is not hypothetical: the Enforcement Directorate already forced Vedanta to refund ₹1,030cr of brand fee in 2023 after finding the same pattern problematic once before. On top of that: a live GAAR finding by India's tax department that VRL's Mauritius holding vehicle was structured mainly to avoid tax (~₹1,308cr exposure); a shareholder PIL now before the Supreme Court on the brand-fee arrangement itself; and the 14 April 2026 boiler explosion at the group's Athena Thermal Power Plant that killed roughly 20-24 workers, giving Viceroy fresh, concrete ammunition for its argument that the group treats ESG/safety as an afterthought. Add continuous dilution of VEDL's stake in its own best asset - a 1.59% HZL OFS in January 2026, with a further ~2% government stake sale reportedly under consideration - and residual shareholders are watching their claim on the crown jewel shrink even as the extraction mechanism that funds the parent survives. None of this shows up in a PE ratio, but all of it is real, current and unresolved.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ₹257.9/share (16 Jul 2026), Vedanta Ltd's market cap is ~₹1,00,849cr; adding ~$1bn (~₹8,300cr) of residual net debt gives an EV of roughly ₹1,09,000cr. Against our estimate of the residual entity's current EBITDA run-rate (63.4% of HZL's record ₹22,162cr FY26 EBITDA ≈ ₹14,050cr, plus copper/nickel/ferrochrome/Zinc International - our own estimate; the company does not disclose the residual-entity split at this granularity - roughly ₹16,000-19,000cr all-in), that implies an EV/EBITDA of about 5.7-6.8x. That looks statistically cheap for a 50%+-margin, 0.4x-levered business, but the EBITDA base it is measured against is a cyclical peak - silver drove 45% of HZL's FY26 profit in a year silver ran hard, and the $959/t zinc cost is a 5-year low, not a sustainable run-rate. Cycle-adjusted toward mid-cycle metal prices, the multiple moves from 'cheap' to 'roughly fair.' Management's own $5bn group-EBITDA-by-2030 target requires more than doubling the current base, resting on a '3 million tonnes zinc+lead by 2031' volume goal that has slipped for a decade, plus speculative early-stage bets with no near-term earnings contribution. We would not pay a premium for that materializing on schedule, and at a fair-not-cheap multiple, the unresolved governance/tax/safety overhang is not being compensated for by the price - dividend yield historically run at a payout ratio near or above 100% of reported EPS on the old consolidated entity, a classic sign that distributions were leverage- rather than earnings-funded, and that pattern is exactly what the parent's continuing brand-fee extraction perpetuates in the new structure.
